newsitem.title: UK: UKs Blair hits trail to catch floating voters.
newsitem.headline: UKs Blair hits trail to catch floating voters.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair on Monday took his election campaign on the road to meet the floating voters he needs to end Labour's 18 years in the political wilderness.
"I think this election will be a battle between hope and fear," he told voters gathered in a hotel ballroom in the cathedral city of Gloucester.
But he would not be sucked into any rash election pledges: "We will not promise to do everything, just those things we can deliver."

His audience for the round table were 20 voters who at the last 1992 election did not pick Labour, overwhelming opinion poll favourites to topple Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conservatives on May 1.
Blair has ditched much socialist dogma in his bid to make a centrist Labour attractive to the middle class voters he needs in marginal seats like Gloucester.
He told the 20 hand-picked voters he hoped would become Labour converts: "I do not think there is any danger of Labour reverting to the past. But I think the challenge is to prove that in office."
Tracey Colbert-Smith, 32, admitted she was too busy chasing her 10-month-old son Samuel to listen to politicians in what will be the longest election campaign of the last 80 years.
She said she would not make her mind up until she gets into the polling booth on election day.

Blair adopted a low-key approach, telling the undecided: "One of the things I want to do is to get out and talk to people, not in a presidential style of glitz and glamour, but just talk to the people about the things that worry you about the country."
Gloucester is symbolically crucial for Blair. It is one of the top 46 marginal seats. A swing to Labour in Gloucester would translate nationwide into a majority of one in parliament.
"Gloucester is an important symbol. If we are to win this constituency, it would give us a majority," Blair said.

Asked about comparison's drawn between America's leading couple, Bill and Hilary Clinton, and himself and his wife Cherie, Blair said: "Well, our wives are both lawyers but there are a lot of them in the world. I am very happy to be compared to the President of the United States but I think the system's very different."
